column3: A wooded hill on the west bank of the Xiang River, with temples, pavilions, an old academy and walking paths overlooking Changsha.
One of the oldest academies in China, founded in 976 and still a place of study after about a thousand years, with halls and courtyards.
A long island in the Xiang River, with parks and a giant statue of the young Mao Zedong carved in stone, and fireworks in the evening.
The museum holds the finds from the Han tomb at Mawangdui, including a silk painting and the remarkably preserved body of Lady Dai.
A stone-paved lane of old shops, tea houses and snack stalls in Changsha, with a flavor of the old city.
A tower on a remnant of the old city wall in the middle of Changsha, with a view of the city's growth.
Fermented tofu fried until crisp, with a strong smell and a rich flavor, served with a spicy dip. A Changsha street classic.
A steamed fish head under a bright red blanket of chopped chilies. It is spicy, tender and one of Hunan's best-known dishes.
Crayfish stir-fried with chili, garlic and spices, and eaten by hand on summer nights in Changsha.
Hot sticky rice cakes fried and dipped in sugar syrup. They are a sweet street snack of Changsha.
Rice noodles in a flavorful pork broth, with toppings such as minced meat, and a typical breakfast in Changsha.
Pork belly braised slowly in soy sauce and sugar until it is soft and glossy. A classic of Hunan home cooking.
Xiang embroidery uses very fine silk thread in shaded colors to make lifelike tigers, flowers and landscapes, one of the four great styles of Chinese embroidery.
Thousands of quartz sandstone pillars rise out of green forest, shrouded in mist. This landscape inspired the floating mountains in a famous film, and it is a UNESCO site.
A mountain with a huge natural arch known as Heaven's Gate, reached by a long cable car and a winding road with 99 bends.
A high area of the park with dense groups of stone pillars, which offers panoramas over the forest.
A glass elevator on the side of a cliff, taking visitors up almost 330 meters in about a minute.
A huge cave system with an underground river, large halls and impressive rock formations.
A very long glass-floored bridge that spans a deep gorge, with a view straight down to the bottom.
A hearty hotpot of meat, tofu and vegetables that is cooked at the table and enjoyed by Tujia families.
Pork cured and smoked over a wood fire by the Tujia people, with a deep, smoky flavor.
Wooden houses on stilts line the Tuo River, with old gates and stone streets. At night, lanterns light up the water.
The home of Shen Congwen, the writer who described Fenghuang's people and landscape and made the town famous.
A covered bridge with shops and teahouses inside, and a popular place to watch the river.
Ginger candy stretched by hand into long strips, with a spicy sweet taste. A traditional treat in Fenghuang.
A spicy Miao-style duck stir-fried with rice cake, chili and herbs, bold and flavorful.
Fabric tied in knots and dipped in indigo dye, so it forms blue-and-white patterns, a traditional craft of the Miao and Tujia peoples.
A tall wooden tower beside Dongting Lake, one of the Three Great Towers of southern China, praised in a famous essay by the Song statesman Fan Zhongyan.
One of the biggest freshwater lakes in China, with broad water, reeds and many birds, flowing into the Yangtze.
A yellow tea of silvery buds, grown on Junshan island in Dongting Lake. Its leaves stand upright in the glass.
Tiny, clear fish from the lake, cooked with egg or in soup, light and tender.
A farmhouse in Shaoshan, where Mao Zedong was born in 1893. It is now a museum, with a pond and fields.
Pork belly braised in soy sauce and sugar until it melts in the mouth. It is said to have been a favorite of Mao.
Mount Heng in the south is one of the Five Sacred Mountains of China, with temples, old pines and mist.
A large temple complex at the foot of Mount Heng, the biggest on the mountain, with a mix of Taoist and Buddhist halls.
Rice noodles in a rich fish broth with chili, a typical dish of Hengyang.
A town in the mountains built beside a waterfall, which became famous from a film of the 1980s.
Fish fermented with rice and salt in jars, and eaten by Miao and Dong people, with a sour taste.
Pork cured with salt and smoked over a fire, hung in kitchens, and cooked with vegetables and chilies.
A duck stir-fried in a pot with chili and its own blood, a spicy, rich dish of Yongzhou.
A garden in Changde said to be the inspiration for Tao Yuanming's story of a hidden paradise among peach blossoms.
A bowl of rice noodles topped with beef or pork in a spicy broth, a Changde breakfast.
